Viral Diseases in Chilli

Leaf Curl Virus and Mosaic Viruses are devastating. They are transmitted by vectors like Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), Thrips, and Aphids. Management: Raise nursery under net house (40-50 mesh). Plant border rows of sorghum/maize as barrier crops. Uproot and destroy infected plants early. Use sticky traps and control vectors using Imidacloprid or Spiromesifen.

Nutrient Management in Chilli

Apply 25 tonnes/ha FYM as basal. Recommended NPK is 120:60:60 kg/ha for irrigated crops. Apply half N, full P, and half K at transplanting. Remaining N and K in two equal splits at 30 and 60 days after transplanting. Foliar application of micronutrients (Zinc, Boron) improves fruit set and quality.

Aflatoxin Management in Chilli

Aflatoxin is produced by Aspergillus flavus during post-harvest handling due to high moisture. Harvest fully mature red fruits. Dry immediately on clean tarpaulins or cemented floors, not directly on soil. Dry until moisture is less than 10%. Avoid mechanical damage to pods during picking and transport.

Chilli Cultivation Guidelines

Climate and Soil
Chilli is a tropical and sub-tropical plant. It grows well in warm and humid climates and dry weather during fruit maturation. A temperature range of 20-25°C is ideal for growth. Frost is detrimental. Well-drained, well-aerated, sandy loam or clay loam soils rich in organic matter are preferred. The optimal soil pH is 6.5 to 7.5.

Nursery Management
Seeds should be treated with beneficial microbes (like Trichoderma) to prevent damping-off disease. Raised beds are recommended for the nursery to prevent water stagnation. Seedlings are ready for transplanting in 4-5 weeks.

Transplanting
Transplant seedlings in the main field at appropriate spacing (e.g., 60x45 cm or 75x60 cm depending on the variety and soil fertility).

Irrigation
Chilli cannot withstand heavy moisture or drought. Frequent and light irrigation is recommended. Drip irrigation is highly efficient and recommended to save water and improve yield.

Harvesting
For green chillies, harvest when fruits are fully mature but still green. For dry chillies, harvest when fruits turn dark red and are slightly wrinkled. Dry the red chillies under the sun until the moisture content is reduced to 10-12%.

Cotton Harvesting and Defoliation

Defoliation is used to induce leaf fall, facilitating cleaner mechanical or manual picking. Ethephon or Thidiazuron can be applied when 60-70% of bolls are open. Picking should be done in the morning. To maintain quality, do not mix different pickings. Kapas must have less than 8% moisture before storage.

Cotton Cultivation in Telangana/AP

Sow high-density planting system (HDPS) with specific short-duration varieties (e.g., ADB 542). Recommended spacing for HDPS is 60x15 cm or 90x15 cm. Nitrogen application must be optimized to prevent excessive vegetative growth. Use Mepiquat Chloride at 45-60 days to regulate growth.

Cotton Cultivation Practices
Climate and Soil
Cotton is a semi-xerophyte. It requires a minimum temperature of 15°C for germination. Optimum temperature for vegetative growth is 21-27°C. It can tolerate temperatures up to 43°C. It requires a frost-free period of 180-200 days. Deep, well-drained, fertile soils with good water holding capacity are ideal. Black cotton soils (Regur) are highly suitable.

Varieties
Selection of varieties should be based on the agro-climatic zone. Short duration varieties are preferred for rainfed conditions to escape terminal drought.

Land Preparation
Deep summer ploughing is recommended to expose resting stages of pests like bollworms and to destroy perennial weeds. Followed by 2-3 harrowings to bring the soil to a fine tilth.

Sowing
Sowing should be taken up with the onset of monsoon in rainfed areas. In irrigated areas, sowing can be pre-poned.
Spacing varies with the variety, soil type, and region (e.g., 90x60 cm or 120x60 cm for hybrids).

Weed Management
Maintain a weed-free environment for the first 60 days. Inter-cultivation and hand weeding are effective.

Harvesting
Picking should be done in the morning hours to avoid dry leaves sticking to the lint. Kapas should be dried in the shade before storage.

Integrated Pest Management (IPM) in Cotton

Major Pests
1. Sucking pests: Jassids, Aphids, Thrips, Whitefly.
2. Bollworms: American bollworm, Pink bollworm, Spotted bollworm.

IPM Strategies
- Deep summer ploughing to destroy pupae of bollworms.
- Grow trap crops like Marigold, Castor, or Pigeonpea around and within the cotton field to attract bollworms and Spodoptera.
- Avoid late sowing.
- Use yellow sticky traps and pheromone traps for monitoring and mass trapping of pests.
- Encourage natural enemies like Ladybird beetles, Chrysoperla, and Trichogramma egg parasitoids.
- Neem-based formulations can be sprayed as a deterrent.
- Chemical pesticides should only be used as a last resort when the pest population crosses the Economic Threshold Level (ETL).

Disease Management in Groundnut

Major diseases include Tikka (Leaf Spot), Rust, and Collar Rot. For Collar Rot (Aspergillus niger), treat seeds with Tebuconazole or Trichoderma. For Leaf Spot and Rust, spray Chlorothalonil or Hexaconazole at 30, 45, and 60 days if symptoms appear. Crop rotation and field sanitation are critical.

Aflatoxin Management in Groundnut

Avoid end-of-season drought stress, as it exacerbates Aspergillus flavus infection. Harvest at correct maturity (when 75-80% pods have dark inner linings). Cure pods rapidly to reduce moisture below 8%. Remove damaged or immature pods before storage. Store in well-ventilated godowns on pallets.

Groundnut Agronomy and Cultivation

Climate and Soil
Groundnut requires abundant sunshine and a warm climate. A temperature range of 25-30°C is ideal for growth. It requires a well-distributed rainfall of 500-700 mm during the vegetative and reproductive phases. Well-drained, light sandy loam or loamy soils are best suited, as they facilitate easy peg penetration and pod development. Heavy clay soils are unsuitable because they restrict pod formation and make harvesting difficult.

Seed Treatment
Treat seeds with appropriate bio-fungicides (like Trichoderma viride) to manage seed and soil-borne diseases. Seed inoculation with Rhizobium culture is recommended to enhance nitrogen fixation.

Sowing
Sowing is usually done with the onset of the monsoon (Kharif season) or in the Rabi/Summer season under assured irrigation. Maintain optimal spacing (e.g., 30x10 cm for bunch types).

Sowing
Sowing is usually done with the onset of the monsoon (Kharif season) or in the Rabi/Summer season under assured irrigation. Maintain optimal spacing (e.g., 30x10 cm for bunch types).

Nutrient Management
Apply well-rotted Farm Yard Manure (FYM). Gypsum application is crucial during the flowering or pegging stage as it provides calcium and sulphur, which are essential for proper pod filling and increasing oil content.

Irrigation
Critical stages for irrigation are flowering, pegging, and pod development. Moisture stress during these stages drastically reduces yield.

Aerobic system of Rice cultivation

Technology Profile
Aerobic rice is a viable option where the shortage of water does not allow the growing of lowland rice. It is growing rice like an upland crop, such as wheat, on non-flooded aerobic soils without stress, thereby eliminating continuous seepage and percolation and greatly reducing evaporation.

Brief description of the technology
The cultivation package developed, recommended, demonstrated and implemented by the farmers included:
- High yielding drought tolerant short duration varieties e.g., DRRDhan42, DRRDhan 44 and DRRDhan46 @20-30kg/ha seed rate
- Well ploughed, and no or very little clods/clumps in field is required like any dry land crops.
- Sowing by dibbling or drilling at 2-3 cm depth, at a spacing of 20-25 X5cm for HYVs and 25-30X10 cm for Hybrids.

- Sowing by dibbling or drilling at 2-3 cm depth, at a spacing of 20-25 X5cm for HYVs and 25-30X10 cm for Hybrids.
- Pre-sowing herbicide application of Glyphophate @2.5 to 5 l/ha in the main field 15 days before field preparation. Application of pendimethalin @ /ha within 3 days of sowing and penoxsulam+cyhalotofop butyl @2.5 l/ha. at 20-30 DAS (2-4 leaf stage of weeds) 50% Nitrogen should be applied at 10-12 days after rice emergence, 25% at maximum vegetative stage (45 DAS), 25% N, 25% K at 50% flowering stage is recommended. If Iron deficiency is noticed, spraying of ferrous sulphate @2.0% ferrous sulphate 3 to 4 times at weekly interval.
- Upon noticing visible symptoms of hairline cracks on soil surface, irrigation is needed to maintain soil at field capacity. Maintenance of saturated condition at critical stages of Active Tillering, Panicle Initiation, Flowering to grain filling stage is essential.
- Need based application of plant protection chemicals

Context
Need: This can increase cropping intensity and income by growing short duration aerobic rice in kharif and safflower/sunflower in early rabi and vegetables in summer season where water scarcity, labor scarcity, high labor wages and poor economic status of farmers is a problem.
Existing practices: When water is limited farmers donot grow rice though they are in need of the staple Crop. Majority of the rice farmers practice flooding irrigation.
Areas: Wasting of precious water with wrong notion that flooding is compulsory for rice. In majority of the rice growing areas in Telangana and Andhrapradesh.

Empirical Evidences
Demonstration yields and incomes
- Water saving of 30 to 56% compared to conventional flooded irrigation. Aerobic rice requires only 470 to 644 mm water
- By reduced cost of cultivation with Opportunity costs with fertilizers, pesticides
- By way of increasing cropping intensity, crop productivity and income

Integrated Pest Management in Rice

Major Pests:
1. Yellow Stem Borer: Causes 'dead hearts' in vegetative stage and 'whiteheads' in reproductive stage. Management involves clipping seedling tips, using light traps, and applying Cartap Hydrochloride or Chlorantraniliprole at ETL.
2. Brown Planthopper (BPH): Causes hopper burn. Manage by avoiding excess nitrogen, providing alternate wetting and drying, and spraying Pymetrozine or Dinotefuran at ETL.
3. Rice Leaf Folder: Causes folded leaves. Manage using Trichogramma chilonis and spraying Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) 5%.

Major Diseases:
1. Blast: Diamond-shaped lesions. Manage with Tricyclazole.
2. Bacterial Leaf Blight (BLB): Yellowish stripes on leaves. Manage using resistant varieties (e.g., Improved Samba Mahsuri) and avoiding excess nitrogen.

Nutrient Management for Rice

Apply NPK based on soil test results. General recommendation is 100-120 kg N, 40-60 kg P2O5, and 40 kg K2O per hectare. Nitrogen should be applied in 3 splits (basal, active tillering, and panicle initiation). Zinc deficiency (Khaira disease) is common in flooded rice; apply Zinc Sulphate at 25 kg/ha if soil is deficient. Use Leaf Color Chart (LCC) for real-time nitrogen management.

Water Management in Rice

Maintain shallow submergence (2-3 cm) during the vegetative stage. Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) is recommended to save 20-30% water without yield penalty. Maintain 5 cm water depth during critical stages: panicle initiation, flowering, and grain filling. Drain the field 10-15 days before harvest to facilitate easy harvesting.

SRI method for resource conservation, profitability and sustainable rice production

Technology Profile
The future of country's rice production will depend heavily on developing and adopting strategies and practices that use irrigation water efficiently at the farm level. System of Rice Intensification (SRI) is one such method which has a potential to produce more rice with less water. Until 1990, the impression was that rice yields better only under flooded conditions. Hence, Water saving technologies in rice is the need of the hour and SRI method which had been tested for last one decade at IIRR and AICRIP programme is one technology which can save resources to more than 30%.

Context
Need: Increase productivity, reduced cost of cultivation, enhancing the soil productivity Existing practices- Majority of the rice farmers practice flooded rice cultivation which consumes 1200 mm ha of water
Potential losses: Water losses, productivity and profitability to an extent of 30% 
Areas: In majority of the rice growing areas in Telangana and Andhrapradesh especially suited for Bore well 46% (DRR, 2005-2014)

Empirical Evidences
Demonstration yields and incomes
SRI spaces rice plants more widely and does not depend on continuous flooding of rice fields. It uses lesser seed, chemical inputs and promotes soil biotic activities in and around the root zone, due to liberal applications of compost and weeding with a rotating hoe that aerates the soil. These changed practices with lower inputs lead to enhanced yields with considerable savings of inputs especially the water which is becoming scarce over the years. Grain yield increase by 10-25% and water use decreased by 29%.

Practical utility/Scalability
- Saving in seed cost to the extent of 60%
- Improved soil health due to use of orgnaics
- Reduced incidence of pests and diseases
- Eco-friendly method of rice cultivation
- Most suited for hybrid rice cultivation and quality seed production
- Already the Practice is followed in 53 countries across the world
- A million farmers in India are practicing the principles of SRI method

Soil Health and Management

Maintain soil organic carbon above 0.5% through crop residue incorporation, green manuring, and application of FYM/compost. Monitor soil pH and electrical conductivity (EC). Reclaim acidic soils with lime and alkaline/sodic soils with gypsum based on Soil Health Card (SHC) recommendations.

Government Schemes for Farmers

1. PM-KISAN: Provides Rs. 6000 per year in three equal installments to eligible landholding farmer families.
2. PMFBY (Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana): Provides insurance cover against crop failure due to natural calamities, pests, and diseases.
3. PKVY (Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana): Promotes organic farming through cluster approach and Participatory Guarantee System (PGS) certification.

Telangana Agricultural Schemes

Rythu Bandhu: Provides investment support for agriculture and horticulture crops by way of a grant of Rs. 5,000 per acre per season to farmers for the purchase of inputs like seeds, fertilizers, and pesticides.
Rythu Bima: Provides Rs. 5 lakhs insurance to the families of deceased farmers irrespective of the cause of death.

Maize Cultivation

Maize is sensitive to both moisture stress and waterlogging. Ensure proper drainage. Recommended NPK is 120:60:40 kg/ha. Apply Nitrogen in 3 splits. Key pest is Fall Armyworm (FAW). Manage FAW by whorl application of Emamectin Benzoate or Spinetoram.

Onion Cultivation

Sowing is done in Kharif (June-July) or Rabi (Oct-Nov). Transplant 45-day-old seedlings. Avoid excessive nitrogen as it causes thick necks and poor storage quality. Major pests are Thrips (spray Fipronil or Spinosad) and Purple Blotch disease (spray Mancozeb or Tebuconazole).

Sugarcane Production Technology

Planting methods include flat-bed, ridge and furrow, or trench method. Use healthy sets treated with Carbendazim. Intercropping with legumes improves soil health. Earthing up should be done 90-120 days after planting to prevent lodging. Main pests are Early Shoot Borer and Top Borer.

Tomato Cultivation

Raise seedlings in pro-trays under a net house. Transplant 25-30 days old seedlings. Stake the plants to prevent fruit contact with soil. Drip irrigation and fertigation are highly recommended. Major pests are Fruit Borer and Whitefly (vector for Leaf Curl Virus).

Wheat Cultivation Guidelines

Optimal sowing time is November. Use high-yielding varieties like HD 2967 or PBW 343. Seed rate is 100 kg/ha. Pre-sowing irrigation is essential. The most critical stage for irrigation is Crown Root Initiation (CRI), which occurs 20-25 days after sowing.

Wheat Diseases

Major diseases include Yellow Rust, Brown Rust, and Karnal Bunt. Yellow Rust causes yellow stripes on leaves. Management involves spraying Propiconazole or Tebuconazole at the first sign of disease. Avoid late sowing to reduce incidence of rusts.
